title: India and China Resume Border Trade at Nathu La Pass After Six-Year Halt
excerpt: Border trade through the historic Silk Route pass in Sikkim restarts August 1, ending a pandemic-era suspension and boosting prospects for local traders and regional connectivity.
body:
• India-China border trade at Nathu La Pass in East Sikkim resumes August 1, ending a six-year suspension since the COVID-19 pandemic.
  • The reopening follows diplomatic agreements from the 2025 Doval-Wang Yi dialogue, which also restored trade at Shipki La and Lipulekh passes.
  • Trade will now be conducted in Indian Rupees and Chinese Yuan, replacing the decades-old barter system.
  • India is investing heavily in road and rail infrastructure in Sikkim, including the Sivok-Rangpo railway link and the Rongli-Menla highway.

Border trade between India and China through the Nathu La Pass in East Sikkim will resume on August 1, marking the end of a six-year suspension triggered by the COVID-19 pandemic. The reopening restores one of the oldest commercial corridors between the two Asian powers — a stretch of the ancient Silk Route that has connected Lhasa to the Indian subcontinent for centuries.

A Trade Route With Deep Roots

The Nathu La border trade point first reopened on July 6, 2006, after being shut for over four decades following the 1962 India-China war. Operating seasonally from May to November each year, it was meant to improve bilateral relations and bring economic activity to remote border communities. The pass sits at roughly 14,140 feet on the Sikkim-Tibet border, part of a route that historically ran from Lhasa through the Chumbi Valley and down to the port of Tamralipta in present-day West Bengal.

But the pandemic halted all activity in 2020, and trade never resumed — even as other aspects of the India-China relationship went through their own turbulence over the Ladakh standoff and broader geopolitical friction.

Diplomatic Thaw Opens Three Passes

The resumption at Nathu La is part of a broader diplomatic package agreed during the 24th round of Special Representatives' dialogue in August 2025, co-chaired by India's National Security Advisor Ajit Doval and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, according to NDTV and the Indian Economic Observer. That meeting produced agreements to reopen border trade at all three designated Himalayan passes: Nathu La in Sikkim, Shipki La in Himachal Pradesh, and Lipulekh in Uttarakhand.

Shipki La already began its 2026 trade season on June 1, with approved traders exchanging 20 designated import items and 36 approved export goods under existing frameworks.

"This is very good news. Trade had been stopped for five years, and many bills remained pending on both sides. The reopening brings hope for us."

— Anil Gupta, trader from Gangtok

From Barter to Currency

One of the most significant changes accompanying the reopening is the shift from barter to currency-based transactions. For centuries, cross-border commerce through the Himalayan passes operated on a barter system — Tibetan traders bringing salt, borax, animal products, and herbs, while Indian traders offered goats, sheep, grains, spices, jaggery, and sugar. Under the new arrangement, trade will be settled in Indian Rupees and Chinese Yuan, a shift that traders have long demanded.

Gangtok-based trader Anil Gupta has also urged authorities to update the 2006 list of tradable goods, suggesting items like sugar and matchsticks be added due to high demand on the Chinese side. Traders have additionally requested more trade passes and the ability to stay overnight at the border, according to the Indian Economic Observer.

Infrastructure Push in Sikkim

India has been investing in connectivity infrastructure that could amplify the impact of reopened trade. The 45-kilometer Sivok-Rangpo railway link is nearing completion, and Indian Railways has started a final location survey for a proposed line linking Gangtok with Nathu La. On the road side, the 93-kilometer Rongli-Menla highway along NH-717B is under construction, connecting Rongli Bazar to Menla near the Indo-Tibet border. The Centre allocated ₹770 crore earlier this year to widen and upgrade NH-717A for better connectivity to the China border.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora, particularly those with roots in Sikkim and the northeastern states, the reopening carries both economic and cultural significance. The Kailash Mansarovar Yatra — one of the most important Hindu pilgrimages — already resumed through Nathu La in 2025 after its own pandemic-era pause. The revival of trade alongside the pilgrimage route signals a broader normalization of activity along this historically charged border.

What's Next

The August 1 restart covers the current May-to-November trading season. Whether the renewed momentum translates into meaningful economic gains will depend on several factors: how quickly the updated trade lists are finalized, whether infrastructure projects stay on schedule, and how the broader India-China relationship evolves. The boundary dispute in several areas of Sikkim remains unresolved, but traders on both sides appear ready to move forward regardless.
nri_angle: The reopening revives trade and pilgrimage routes significant to Indians with roots in Sikkim and the northeast, following the 2025 resumption of the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra through the same pass.
